column1: Use this sheet to track completion of each project management step during your project.

column4: What to Do
Recognize a business need, problem, or opportunity that requires a project. Confirm it is not just an ongoing operationa...
Write a clear project purpose statement that explains WHY the project exists and WHAT success looks like in simple terms...
Formally assign an executive sponsor who owns the project, removes obstacles, and champions the work.
Define what is IN scope and explicitly what is OUT of scope to prevent scope creep.
List everyone who is affected by or can affect the project. Understand their level of interest and influence.
Establish measurable criteria that will determine whether the project has been completed successfully.
Summarize the project purpose, scope, sponsor, high-level timeline, and resources in a single reference document. Get fo...
Decompose the total project scope into smaller, manageable deliverables and work packages.
List all specific tasks needed to complete each deliverable and identify dependencies between tasks.
Estimate how much effort (person-hours) and elapsed time (days/weeks) each task will require.
Assign Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed roles for every key task and decision.
Combine tasks, sequences, and estimates into a timeline. Identify the critical path.
Identify people, materials, tools, and costs needed. Create a budget aligned to the schedule.
Brainstorm potential risks that could derail the project. Prioritize by likelihood and impact.
For each high-priority risk, define a mitigation strategy (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept).
Identify who needs what information, in what format, and how often. Set up reporting cadence.
Present the full project plan to the sponsor and key stakeholders for formal approval before work begins.
Bring the full team together to align on the plan, roles, expectations, and ways of working.
Apply FranklinCovey's 4 Disciplines of Execution: set WIGs, keep scoreboard, hold team accountable.
Team members carry out assigned tasks according to the plan, producing the agreed deliverables.
Confirm that work meets quality standards through reviews, testing, and inspections as work progresses.
Keep stakeholders informed and engaged. Address concerns early to maintain support and minimize surprises.
If vendors or contractors are needed, manage selection, contracting, and performance.
Regularly compare actual progress (% complete, tasks done) against the baseline schedule.
Track spending against the approved budget. Identify variances early and determine corrective actions.
Hold regular team and stakeholder status meetings to surface issues, decisions, and blockers.
Log, assign, and resolve issues. Escalate to sponsor when decisions exceed PM authority.
Revisit the risk register regularly. Close resolved risks, add new risks, update probabilities.
Evaluate all requested changes to scope, schedule, or cost. Approve or reject through a formal process.
When approved changes or variances require it, update the schedule, budget, or resource plan formally.
Confirm that all project deliverables have been produced, meet acceptance criteria, and are complete.
Get written sign-off from the sponsor and/or customer that the project is complete and acceptable.
Hand off the deliverable to the people who will own and operate it going forward. Provide training if needed.
Facilitate a retrospective with the team to capture what went well, what didn't, and what to do differently.
Organize and store all project documents in a central location for future reference and organizational learning.
Formally release team members from project duties, update their managers, and return equipment/licenses.
Summarize project performance: scope achieved, budget vs. actuals, schedule vs. baseline, lessons learned.
Acknowledge the team's effort and contribution. Celebrate wins to build morale and culture.
